PREFACE
India’s West Coast is bordered by the Western Ghats, which occupy a region of 180000
square kilometers. A mega biodiversity zone and biodiversity hotspot with a wide
variety of flora, fauna, and landscape are known as the “Western Ghats”. The Western
Ghats have exceptionally high levels of endemicity and plant and animal variety, as
well as a significant number of species that are threatened with extinction
internationally. The natural ecosystems of this hotspot are in danger due to the adverse
effects of human activity on the environment, so immediate conservation measures are
required, particularly the expansion of the protected area network. The chance to profit
from biodiversity to the fullest possible will be lost forever if no steps are done to
preserve it. The area is also home to several nationally notable animal sanctuaries, tiger
reserves, and national parks, as well as a good collection of large mammals. Find
numerous medicinal plants as well as significant genetic resources, such as wild
relatives of cereals, fruits, and spices available in the Western Ghats. The Western
Ghats are home to a variety of social, religious, and linguistic groups in addition to a
rich biodiversity. This book primarily focuses on the diversity of floral and specific
faunal elements, especially the bird varieties.
Dr. Sr. Beena Jose
Principal
Vimala College (Autonomous),

THE NILGIRIS: A BIOGEOGRAPHIC HOTSPOT FOR THE
ORCHID DIVERSITY
1K. Kiruthika, 2M. Sulaiman and 3P.B. Harathi
1Department of Botany, PSGR Krishnammal College for Women, Peelamedu,
Coimbatore 641 004, Tamil Nadu
2Botanical Survey of India, Southern Regional Centre, Coimbatore 641 002, Tamil
Nadu
3Department of Zoology, PSGR Krishnammal College for Women, Peelamedu,
Coimbatore 641 004, Tamil Nadu
Corresponding author:kiruthika.zizyphus@gmail.com
1.1. INTRODUCTION
Orchidaceae, one of the diversified group among the angiosperms is
distributed with ca. 28,000 taxa in tropics, sub-tropics and temperate regions of the
world. They are known to occupy a variety of niches with habitats ranging from
terrestrial to epiphytic and even underground (Christenhusz & Byng 2016, Adit &
al. 2021). While our country, India experience the Tropical wet and dry climate with
varied topographic factors thus flourishing the terrain into ten biogeographic regions.
These influence the country for rich biodiversity with 11.4% of the total species from
earth. Among these, Indian orchids is recorded with 1268 taxa of 155 genera with
307 endemics (Singh & al. 2020). Also, the orchids are rare with limited population
due to high environmental threats viz. habitat loss, land use change, road expansion,
and pollution. Therefore, the Orchidaceae family is recognised as Threatened Group
of flowering plants.
1.2. The Nilgiris of the Western Ghats
The Western Ghats is one of the four Biodiversity Hotspots in India, running
parallel to the Arabian coast from 8˚N to 21˚N latitude covering 1,60,000 km2. These
undulating mountains are distributed in the States of Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa,
Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. Amidst a Palghat gap with 30 km wide interrupt

Biodiversity of Western Ghats ISBN: 978-81-960780-0-3
the continuous chain of hills between Nilgiris and Anamalais. Due to high floristic
richness and high concentration of endemic plants Western Ghats is divided into two
sub-divisions as northern Western Ghats [includes Konkan and Raigad-Khandala
Hills; and Shimoga-Chikmagalur-Dakshina Kannada of Karnataka] and southern
Western Ghats [includes Malabar coast and Northern Kodagu; and Nilgiri-Wayanad-
Silent Valley plateau and hills; Palni hills; Anamalai and High range hills;
Agasthyamalai-Tirunelveli and Mahendragiri hills].
Besides various regions in the Western Ghats, The Nilgiris is endowed with unique
feature of topography and climate. Based on this, the area is divided into The Nilgiri
Plateau (central part), The Sigur Plateau (lying at the foot hills on the northern side
of the former), The Nilgiri-Wayanad (lying on the western side of the above two
plateau) and the outer slopes facing the plains (Sharma et al. 1977, Joseph 1987).
The Nilgiris District lies in the state of Tamil Nadu positioned at 11°12 N - 11°37 N
Latitude and 76°30 E - 76°55 E Longitude with the altitude between 300-2,637 m
and covering geographical area about 2,565 km2; very dense forest, moderate dense
forest and open forest with 460.67 km2, 629.51 km2 and 641.20 km2 respectively. It
is bounded on the north by Karnataka state, south-west by Kerala and; east and south-
east by Coimbatore District, Tamil Nadu. Almost all important forest types of south
India are represented here viz. Southern Tropical Thorn Forests, Southern Tropical
Dry Deciduous Forests, Southern Tropical Moist Deciduous Forests, Tropical Semi-
Evergreen Forests, Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests, Sub-tropical Hill Savannah and
Southern Montane Wet Temperate Forests (Champion and Seth 1968) are distributed
from the elevation 300-2,637 m.
1.3. The Nilgiris favours orchid diversity
The Nilgiris is the treasure hunt for the Naturalist; diversified with rich flora
and fauna. For this reason, The Protected Areas was formed in Nilgiri and declared
as Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve in 1986 covering an area about 5,520 km2, Mukurthi
- 33 -

Biodiversity of Western Ghats ISBN: 978-81-960780-0-3
National Park with 78.46 km2 in 1982 and Mudumalai Tiger Reserve with 321 km2
in 2007. The Nilgiris is recognised as one of the highest rich biodiversity regions of
the Western Ghats; and favourable habitation of orchid diversity with 138 species of
51 genera (Table 1 & Plates 1-7). The endemism accounts with 55 species to the
study area (40 species endemic to the Western Ghats, 07 species endemic to the
Eastern and Western Ghats, 03 species endemic to Tamil Nadu, and 05 species
distributed throughout India). This is due to a distinct geographical location,
topography, wide range of altitudinal variations from 700 – 2637 m, marked climate
regimes, significant diurnal range of solar radiation and temperature (Singh & al.
2015). These factors determine the orchid diversity on each zonation of vegetation;
where the species richness increases along the altitude and in mid elevation peak the
diversity is high having an empirical support for the species (Rahbek 1995).
1.4. Risk factors for orchid survival
Besides its unique distribution pattern, the orchids face high risk for its
survival from habitat loss, torrential rainfall, landslides, encroachment, over
exploitation for medicinal purposes, road extension, and pollution etc., Therefore an
urgent need for raising the awareness on orchid should be dispersed among the
public, school and college students, and local people. This could be facilitated
through participatory approach. The community participation (local people) helps to
recognise the importance of orchids and wealth of their own forests. It benefits with
conservation of orchids and biodiversity of an area which contributes towards the
Sustainable Development Goals (SDG’s).
